sessions.title: 是: A is B
sessions.focus: Saying who or what someone is: 我是…, 他不是…
sessions.goal: Say who someone is: 我是学生, 他不是老师.

blocks.text: To say who or what someone is, put 是 (shì) between the two: **A 是 B**. It's *am, is, are* in English, *bin, ist, sind* in German.

ex.note: 我妈妈 = my mum (more in G05).

blocks.text: Chinese verbs have no endings: 是 is the same for *I, you, he, we, they*, and the same for *was* and *will be*. There's no word for *a* or *the* either, and no plural ending: 孩子 is *child* or *children*.
For *is not*, put 不 (bù) before 是. Before 是 it's said **bú**, because 是 is a 4th tone (G04 explains this).

ex.note: 先生 = Mr, sir, or husband.

blocks.text: 是 links two *things*: people, jobs, names. It doesn't go before words like *good, busy, big*. Those work differently (G03).

wrong.why: For *I'm fine*, say 我很好, without 是 (G03).

blocks.tip: 他 (he) and 她 (she) are both said tā. Only the character tells them apart.

exercises.explain: 不 goes right before 是: 不是.
Between two nouns (我们 and 朋友): 是.

sessions.title: 吗: yes-no questions
sessions.focus: Add 吗 to the end; answer with the verb
sessions.goal: Ask yes-no questions and answer them.

blocks.text: To turn a statement into a yes-no question, add 吗 (ma) at the end. Nothing else moves: no swapping like *Are you…?* or *Bist du…?*

ex.note: Literally *Are you good?*

blocks.tip: 吗 is light: short, without a tone of its own. The question is in the word 吗, so your voice doesn't have to go up at the end.

blocks.text: Chinese has no one word for *yes* or *no*. Answer with the verb of the question: 是 or 不是, 去 or 不去, 知道 or 不知道. When someone checks a fact, 对 (duì, *right*) also works as *yes*.

wrong.why: 吗 goes at the very end: 你是学生吗？

exercises.explain: 吗 goes at the very end, nothing else moves.

words.english: (turns a sentence into a yes/no question)
to have; there is / there are

sessions.title: 很 + adjective
sessions.focus: 我很好: adjectives work like verbs, no 是
sessions.goal: Say how someone or something is: 我很好, 他很忙.

blocks.text: Words like *good, busy, big* (adjectives) work like verbs in Chinese. 好 isn't just *good*, it's *to be good*, so there's no 是. But a bare 我好 sounds like a comparison (*I'm the good one*), so a plain statement puts 很 (hěn) in front.

ex.note: Three 3rd tones in a row: the first two are said as 2nd tones, wó hén hǎo.

ex.english: There are a lot of people.
ex.note: Literally *people are many*: 多 is an adjective, too.

blocks.text: 很 means *very*, but here it's mostly glue: 我很好 is just *I'm fine*. To really mean *very*, stress 很, or say 非常 (fēicháng).

wrong.why: 是 links two nouns (G01). Adjectives don't need it: 我很好.
Say 她很忙.

blocks.text: For *not*, 不 takes the place of 很. In a 吗 question, 很 usually drops out too.

blocks.tip: Think of 忙 as *to be busy* and 高兴 as *to be happy*. Then 我很忙 is simply *I (very) am-busy*.

exercises.explain: Adjectives don't take 是: 他很忙.

exercises.english: There are a lot of people.

sentence.english: There are a lot of people.

exercises.explain: 多 (many) is an adjective: 人很多.

words.english: (turns a sentence into a yes/no question)

sessions.title: 不: not
sessions.focus: 不 before verbs and adjectives; bù or bú
sessions.goal: Say what isn't so, or what you don't do: 我不知道, 我不去.

blocks.text: 不 (bù) makes a verb or an adjective negative. It goes right before the word it negates.

不 is a 4th tone, **bù**. Before another 4th tone it becomes a 2nd tone, **bú**, because two falling tones in a row are hard to say. Here the change is written in the Pinyin, and you hear it in the audio.

ex.note: 是 is a 4th tone, so bú.
去 is a 4th tone, so bú.
要 is a 4th tone, so bú. 不要 = don't want.
来 is a 2nd tone: 不 stays bù.

blocks.text: 不 says something isn't so, or that you don't (or won't) do it: now, usually, or later. Two cases are different: *didn't* in the past is 没 (G17), and *don't have* is 没有, never 不有 (G08).

ex.english: He doesn't eat it. / He won't eat it.

wrong.why: 不 goes before the verb: 我不知道.
有 takes 没, not 不: 我没有时间 (G08).

blocks.tip: To answer *no*, say 不 + the verb of the question: 不去, 不是, 不知道 (G02).

exercises.explain: 去 is a 4th tone, so 不 is said bú.
不 goes right before the verb.
好 is a 3rd tone, so 不 stays bù.

words.english: to have; there is / there are

sessions.title: 的: my, your, his
sessions.focus: 我的, 你的朋友, and when 的 is left out
sessions.goal: Say whose something is: 我的钱, 你的朋友, 这是我的.

blocks.text: 的 (de) links an owner to what's theirs, like *'s* in English: 我的 = *my*, 你的 = *your*, 他的 = *his*, 妈妈的 = *Mum's*.

ex.pinyin: Zhè shì nǐ de dōngxi ma?
ex.numbers: Zhe4 shi4 ni3 de5 dong1xi5 ma5?

blocks.text: Leave out the thing when it's clear: 我的 alone is *mine*.

blocks.h: Family and close people: no 的

blocks.text: After a pronoun, 的 usually drops out before family and close people: 我妈妈 *my mum*, 我爸爸 *my dad*, 我朋友 *my friend*. With things, keep it: 我的钱.

wrong.why: With things, keep 的: 我的钱.

blocks.tip: 的 is light: short, with almost no weight. It's the most common word in Chinese.

exercises.explain: Owner, then 的, then the thing: 妈妈的钱.
这是我 means *This is me*. *Mine* is 我的.

words.english: (links a describer to a noun): 's, of
(turns a sentence into a yes/no question)

sessions.title: 什么 and 谁: what, who
sessions.focus: Question words stay where the answer goes
sessions.goal: Ask *what* and *who*: 这是什么？ 他是谁？

blocks.text: Questions with 什么 (shénme, *what*) and 谁 (shéi, *who*) keep the normal word order. The question word goes exactly where the answer will go, not to the front as in English and German.

blocks.pattern: 他是谁？ → 他是我朋友。
blocks.english: Who is he? → He's my friend.

ex.note: 谁 is also said shuí. The audio says shuí.

blocks.h: The answer goes in the same place

ex.note: Literally *You're called what name?*

blocks.text: 什么 also goes before a noun: 什么东西 *what thing*, 什么问题 *what question*.
什么 and 谁 already make a question, so there's no 吗.

wrong.why: The question word stays where the answer goes: 这是什么？
Already a question: no 吗.

exercises.explain: No 吗 with 谁, and 谁 goes where the answer goes: 她是我朋友 → 她是谁？

words.english: (links a describer to a noun): 's, of
(turns a sentence into a yes/no question)
to have; there is / there are
to be called; to call, to shout

sessions.title: 这 and 那: this, that
sessions.focus: 这, 那, 这个, 那个, 这里, 那里
sessions.goal: Point at things and places: 这个, 那个, 这里, 那里.

blocks.text: 这 (zhè) is *this*, 那 (nà) is *that*. On their own they start a sentence: 这是… *This is…*, 那是… *That is…*

blocks.h: 这个, 那个: this one, that one

blocks.text: Before a noun, or for *this one*, add 个 (ge): 这个人 *this person*, 那个东西 *that thing*. 个 is a measure word (G10). In speech you'll often hear zhèige and nèige.

ex.note: Literally *this question is good*.

wrong.why: After a verb, say 那个: 我要那个.

blocks.h: 这些, 那些: these, those
这里, 那里: here, there

ex.english: There are a lot of people there.

blocks.tip: 这 (zhè) has the tongue curled back for zh (P05), 那 (nà) the tongue tip behind the teeth for n. Both are 4th tones. Don't mix up 那 with 哪 (nǎ, *which*, G10): same sound, but a 3rd tone.

exercises.explain: After a verb, *this one* is 这个.

sentence.english: There are a lot of people there.

words.english: (links a describer to a noun): 's, of

sessions.title: 有: to have, there is
sessions.focus: 有 and 没有 (never 不有)
sessions.goal: Say what you have and what there is: 我有时间, 这里没有人.

blocks.text: 有 (yǒu) means *to have*.
有 is also *there is, there are*. The place comes first: 这里有人 is *there's someone here*, literally *here has people*. German *es gibt* works the same way, without a *there*.

ex.english: Is anyone here? / Is this seat taken?
There's a lot of stuff there.

blocks.h: Not: 没有, never 不有

blocks.text: 有 is the one verb that doesn't take 不. Its *not* is 没 (méi): 没有 is *don't have* or *there isn't*. In speech 有 often drops: 没钱 = 没有钱.

wrong.why: Never 不有: 我没有时间.

blocks.h: Asking: 吗 or 有没有

blocks.text: Ask with 吗, or with 有没有, *have or not have*, which needs no 吗. The answer is 有 or 没有.

exercises.explain: 有 takes 没, never 不.

exercises.english: There are a lot of people there.

sentence.english: There are a lot of people there.

exercises.explain: *There is / there are* is 有, with the place first.

words.english: at, in; to be (somewhere); (doing) right now
(turns a sentence into a yes/no question)
to have; there is / there are

sessions.title: 在: being somewhere
sessions.goal: Say where someone or something is, and where something happens: 我在家, 我在家工作.

blocks.text: 在 (zài) says where someone or something is: *to be at, to be in*. For places it takes the place of 是.

blocks.english: A is at / in the place

wrong.why: For places, use 在: 我在这里.

ex.note: In the north of China you'll also hear 哪儿 (nǎr).

ex.english: He isn't here. / He's not in.
ex.note: On the phone: *He's not in.*

blocks.text: When something happens at a place, 在 + place comes **before** the verb: *I at home work*, not *I work at home*.

blocks.english: A does it at the place

wrong.why: The place goes before the verb: 我在家工作.

blocks.tip: 在 before a verb without a place means *to be doing* (他在工作, *he's working*). That's G23.

exercises.explain: Where someone is: 在, not 是.
在 + place comes before the verb.

words.english: (links a describer to a noun): 's, of
at, in; to be (somewhere); (doing) right now
to have; there is / there are

sessions.title: Numbers and 个
sessions.focus: 一个人, 两个, 几个, 多少
sessions.goal: Count people and things, and ask how many: 三个孩子, 几个, 多少钱.

blocks.text: The numbers one to ten: 一 yī, 二 èr, 三 sān, 四 sì, 五 wǔ, 六 liù, 七 qī, 八 bā, 九 jiǔ, 十 shí.

Between a number and a noun, Chinese always puts a **measure word**, like *a cup of* or *a piece of* in English, but every time. The most common one, and the one that's never wrong in speech, is 个 (ge).

ex.note: 一个 is said yí ge: 个 is really a 4th tone, so 一 becomes yí.

wrong.why: A measure word is needed: 三个孩子.

blocks.h: Two things: 两, not 二

blocks.text: For two of something, say 两 (liǎng): 两个人. 二 (èr) is for counting out loud, inside longer numbers and for *second*.

wrong.why: For two of something, say 两: 两个孩子.

blocks.h: How many? 几 and 多少

blocks.text: 几 (jǐ) asks *how many* when you expect a small number (under about ten). It takes 个 like a number does. 多少 (duōshao) works for any amount, and can go without 个.

ex.english: How many children do you have?
How much money do you have?

ex.note: The question for prices.

blocks.text: 个 also goes after 这, 那 (G07) and 哪 (nǎ, *which*).

blocks.tip: 一 changes its tone like 不: yī on its own and when counting, yí before a 4th tone (yí ge), yì before the other tones (yì tiān, *one day*).

exercises.explain: Two of something is 两, and number + 个 go before the noun: 两个孩子.

sentence.english: How many children do you have?

exercises.explain: 哪 (nǎ, 3rd tone) asks *which*. 那 (nà, 4th tone) is *that*.

words.english: (links a describer to a noun): 's, of
to have; there is / there are

sessions.title: 想, 要, 喜欢 + verb
sessions.focus: Wanting and liking to do something
sessions.goal: Say what you want and like to do: 我想去, 我喜欢工作.

blocks.text: 想 (xiǎng), 要 (yào) and 喜欢 (xǐhuan) go straight before another verb. There's no *to* in between, just like German *Ich will gehen*.

blocks.pattern: A + 想 / 要 / 喜欢 + verb
blocks.english: A would like to / wants to / likes to …

ex.english: What would you like to eat?

blocks.h: 要: want to, have to, going to

blocks.text: 要 is firmer than 想: *want to*, *need to*, or a plan, *going to*. Before a thing, it's *to want*: 要什么 *want what*.

blocks.h: Not: 不想, 不喜欢, and careful with 不要

blocks.text: Before a verb, 不要 means *don't!* (G30). For *I don't want to*, say 不想.

wrong.why: 想 comes first, then what you want to do: 我想去.

blocks.tip: 想 on its own also means *to think* and *to miss*: 我想你, *I miss you*.

sentence.english: What would you like to eat?

exercises.explain: 不要去 would be *don't go!* For *I don't want to*, say 不想.
喜欢 comes first, then what you like doing.

words.english: to want to; to think; to miss

sessions.title: 会 and 能: can
sessions.focus: Can because you learned it, or because you're able to
sessions.goal: Say what you can do: 我会说中文, 你能来吗？

blocks.text: 会 (huì) and 能 (néng) both mean *can*, but for different reasons. Both go right before the verb.

blocks.h: 会: can, because you learned it

blocks.text: 会 is for skills: languages, cooking, driving, swimming. German has the same word for it: *Ich kann Chinesisch*.

blocks.h: 能: can, because you're able to or allowed

blocks.text: 能 is about the situation: you have the time, you're well enough, it's allowed.

wrong.why: 会 goes right before the verb: 我会说中文.

blocks.tip: 会 also means *will* (他会来的, *he'll come*). That's G56.

exercises.explain: Coming today isn't a skill you learn: 能. (你今天会来吗 would be *Will you come today?*)
不能 goes right before the verb.

words.english: at, in; to be (somewhere); (doing) right now
(turns a sentence into a yes/no question)

sessions.title: Time words come early
sessions.focus: 我今天很忙: when goes before the verb
sessions.goal: Say when something happens: 我今天很忙, 我明天去.

blocks.text: Words for *when* (今天 today, 明天 tomorrow, 现在 now) go **before** the verb: right after the person, or at the very start. Never at the end, as in English *I'm busy today*.

ex.note: Both orders are fine. At the start, the time gets a bit more weight.

wrong.why: Time goes before the verb: 我今天很忙.
Say 我明天去.

blocks.text: With a time and a place, the time comes first: *who, when, where, what*. German is close: *Ich arbeite heute zu Hause*.

ex.note: There's no *will*: 明天 already says it's in the future.

blocks.tip: Chinese verbs don't show the time. Time words like 今天 and 明天, and words like 了 (G17), do that job.

exercises.explain: The time goes before the verb.
The time word goes first, and 几 already makes a question: no 吗.

words.english: at, in; to be (somewhere); (doing) right now
(turns a sentence into a yes/no question)

sessions.title: 呢: and you?
sessions.focus: 你呢? and questions that are already questions
sessions.goal: Ask *and you?* and *where is…?* with 呢.

blocks.text: 呢 (ne) after a person or thing asks *and…?* or *what about…?*: the same question as before, now about someone else.

ex.english: I'm not going. What about him?

blocks.text: Without a question before it, A 呢 asks *where is A?*
At the end of a question with 什么, 谁, 怎么 and so on, 呢 makes it softer, a bit like *then* or *I wonder*. It never goes with 吗.

wrong.why: 吗 and 呢 never go together.

blocks.tip: 呢 is light, like 吗: short, with no tone of its own.

exercises.english: I'm not going. What about you?

sentence.english: I'm not going. What about you?

exercises.explain: *And you?* is 你呢？ 吗 needs a whole sentence before it.

words.english: (links a describer to a noun): 's, of
at, in; to be (somewhere); (doing) right now

sessions.title: 也 and 都: also, all
sessions.focus: Both go right before the verb
sessions.goal: Say *also* and *all*: 我也是学生, 我们都很忙.

blocks.text: 也 (yě, *also, too*) and 都 (dōu, *all, both*) go right **before the verb** or adjective. Never at the start or the end of the sentence.

ex.note: 也不 = not either.

wrong.why: 也 goes after the person, before the verb: 我也是学生.
Not at the end either: 我也是学生.

blocks.text: 都 sums up the people or things **before** it: 我们都 *all of us*, 他们都 *all of them*.

ex.note: 大家 = everyone. *All the people* isn't 都人: 都 looks back.
都不 = all not = none.

blocks.text: Together, 也 comes first.

exercises.explain: 都 goes after the people it sums up, right before 很忙.

options: Not all of them are here.
exercises.explain: 都不 = all not = none.

sessions.title: 和: and
sessions.focus: 和 joins people and things, not sentences
sessions.goal: Say *A and B* and *with someone*: 爸爸和妈妈, 我跟他一起去.

blocks.text: 和 (hé) means *and*, but only between people or things: 我和你 *you and me*, 这个和那个 *this one and that one*. It never joins two sentences.

ex.pinyin: Bàba hé māma dōu zài jiā.
ex.numbers: Ba4ba5 he2 ma1ma5 dou1 zai4 jia1.
ex.english: Dad and Mum are both at home.
I want this one and that one.

blocks.text: To join two sentences, put them side by side with a comma, often with 也 (G15).

ex.pinyin: Wǒ hěn máng, tā yě hěn máng.
ex.numbers: Wo3 hen3 mang2, ta1 ye3 hen3 mang2.
ex.english: I'm busy, and he's busy too.

blocks.h: With: 和, 跟 + 一起

blocks.text: 和 + person + verb is doing something *with* someone, often with 一起 (yìqǐ, *together*). 跟 (gēn) works the same and is more common in speech.

blocks.pattern: A + 和 / 跟 + B + 一起 + verb

blocks.text: Put a list comma (、) between the first ones, and 和 before the last.

ex.pinyin: Wǒ, nǐ hé tā dōu shì xuésheng.
ex.numbers: Wo3, ni3 he2 ta1 dou1 shi4 xue2sheng5.

sessions.title: 了 and 没: it happened, it didn't
sessions.goal: Say that something happened, or didn't: 我吃了, 我没吃.

blocks.text: Chinese verbs don't change for the past. Instead, 了 (le) after a verb says the action happened or is done: 我吃了 *I ate, I've eaten*.

blocks.english: A did it / has done it

ex.note: Literally *now I know*.

blocks.text: With an amount, or a question word, 了 goes right after the verb.

blocks.h: Didn't: 没 + verb, and no 了

blocks.text: For *didn't* or *haven't*, put 没 (méi) or 没有 before the verb, and leave out 了. Not 不: 不 is for now and later (G04).

blocks.english: A didn't do it / hasn't done it

ex.english: I haven't eaten. / I didn't eat.

wrong.why: No 了 with 没: 我没吃.

blocks.text: Ask with 了吗, or with 了没有 at the end (*…or not?*).

ex.note: Also a friendly greeting around mealtimes.

blocks.tip: 了 has a second job, *now it's different* (我不想去了, *I don't want to go any more*). That's G21. For now: 了 after a verb = it happened.

exercises.explain: No 了 with 没. (我不吃了 means *I'm not eating any more*.)
*Didn't* is 没. 他不来 is *he isn't coming*.

words.english: (turns a sentence into a yes/no question)

sessions.title: 太…了: too, so
sessions.goal: Say *too…*, *so…!* and *not very*: 太好了, 太大了, 不太好.

blocks.text: 太 (tài) + adjective + 了 means *too…*, or *so…!* when it's something nice. It's stronger than 很 (G03) and shows how you feel.
Without 了 it sounds unfinished: say 太好了, not just 太好.

wrong.why: Add 了: 太好了！

blocks.text: 不太 + adjective, without 了, is a gentle *not very*. It's how people say something isn't good without sounding harsh.

blocks.tip: 不太 is said bú tài: 太 is a 4th tone (G04).

exercises.explain: *Not very* is 不太, before the word.

sessions.title: 怎么 and 怎么样: how
sessions.focus: How to do something, and how something is
sessions.goal: Ask *how*: 这个怎么说？ 你怎么样？

blocks.text: 怎么 (zěnme) before a verb asks *how* to do something.

wrong.why: 怎么 goes before the verb: 你怎么说？ (For *what did you say?*, it's 你说什么？)

blocks.text: Said with surprise or worry, 怎么 means *how come, why*.

ex.note: Literally *How come you're here?*

blocks.h: 怎么样: how is it? how about…?

blocks.text: 怎么样 (zěnmeyàng) goes at the end. It asks how something is, or suggests something: *how about it?* Answer with an adjective: 很好, 不太好, 太好了!

ex.english: Let's go together, how about it?
I don't know what to do.

exercises.explain: At the end, *how is it?* is 怎么样. 怎么 needs a verb after it.

exercises.explain: 怎么样 goes at the end, after the suggestion.
